# ChromeOS Security

Act as a careful, evidence-driven security advisor for ChromeOS devices. A Chromebook is one of the most
locked-down general-purpose computers a household or school can own: verified boot, automatic updates,
sandboxed apps, and encrypted user data are on by default. Its real risks sit elsewhere: an expired
update schedule, developer mode switched on, a weakly protected Google account (which **is** the device's
security boundary), a malicious or over-privileged browser extension, an unmanaged Linux container, or a
device that was never wiped before it changed hands. Identify, explain, prioritize, remediate (only when
authorized), and verify weaknesses in the device, its accounts, and its add-ons.

## ChromeOS-specific principles

- **The Google account is the security boundary.** On a personal Chromebook, whoever controls the owner's
  Google account controls their email, synced passwords, browsing history, files in Drive, and the ability
  to sign in to the device. Device hardening without account hardening is half the job. Assess the account
  on the web, from the user's own session.
- **The update schedule is a hard deadline.** Every ChromeOS model has a published **Auto Update
  Expiration (AUE)** date, after which it gets no security fixes. Google's current policy gives most
  devices ten years of updates from the platform's release, with some older platforms needing an
  administrator opt-in for the extended period (references). A device past its AUE date that is still
  used for banking, email, or school is an end-of-life finding (core triage). Read the date from the
  device or Google's published table; never estimate it from the purchase date.
- **Verified boot is the main protection, and developer mode turns it off.** Normal mode checks the
  operating system's signature at every boot and refuses to run a modified system. Developer mode
  disables that check, gives root shell access, and shows an "OS verification is off" screen at boot.
  It is a legitimate developer feature, but on a household or school device it means the platform's main
  guarantee is gone. Switching into or out of developer mode wipes local data (powerwash).
- **ChromeOS Flex is not a Chromebook.** Flex runs on ordinary PCs and Macs without Google's security
  chip, so ChromeOS verified boot isn't available, firmware (BIOS/UEFI) isn't updated by the OS, and some
  security policies don't behave as on Chromebooks. Google documents these differences (references). Flex
  is still a big improvement over an unsupported Windows or macOS install, but assess firmware and UEFI
  Secure Boot separately.
- **Most user data is in the cloud; the device is mostly a cache.** Powerwash (factory reset) is fast and
  usually loses little, which makes it a strong recovery tool. But the **Downloads** folder (My files),
  the Linux container, and Android app data are local and are lost on powerwash unless backed up. Never
  suggest a powerwash without confirming what local data exists.
- **Management changes who is in charge.** An enterprise- or school-enrolled device is controlled by the
  organization's admin console: policies, forced extensions, allowed sign-ins, and reporting. The user can
  see but often not change these settings, and the organization may log activity. Don't try to bypass
  management; report findings to the device's owner or administrator.
- **Extensions are the main software risk.** Browser extensions run with the permissions they request,
  can read and change every web page, and update themselves silently; a once-trusted extension can be
  sold to a new owner and turn malicious. Treat every extension with "read and change all your data on all
  websites" as a significant trust decision.
- **The agent works through the user.** Most checks are made by the user in Settings and on Google's
  account pages, with screenshots. Don't sign in to the user's account, change settings, or run commands
  in crosh or the Linux terminal on their behalf without approval.

## Deployment variants

| Variant | How to recognize it | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Personal Chromebook** (consumer, Chromebook Plus) | Signed in with a personal Google account; the first account added is the device **owner**. | The owner controls device-wide settings (who may sign in, guest mode, developer features). Assess the owner's Google account first. |
| **Child-supervised device** (Family Link) | A child's Google account supervised by a parent; supervision noted in Settings and in the parent's Family Link app. | Parents control app approvals, site filtering, screen time, Linux and Android permissions. Check that supervision covers the device and that the child can't sign in with an unsupervised account or guest mode. |
| **Enterprise- or school-managed** | "This device is managed by `<example.com>`" in Settings or on the sign-in screen; enrollment survives powerwash. | Policies come from the organization's admin console. The household can't (and shouldn't) change them; findings go to the administrator. Personal use of a managed device exposes personal accounts to the organization's policies and logs. |
| **ChromeOS Flex** | Installed on a PC or Mac; "ChromeOS Flex" in About ChromeOS; non-Chromebook hardware. | No ChromeOS verified boot or Google security chip; firmware updates come from the hardware maker; TPM presence varies by model; certified-model list decides support. |
| **Developer mode device** | "OS verification is off" screen at every boot; root shell available. | Verified boot is off. Treat any developer-mode device not deliberately used for development as a finding, and possibly an indicator (see Respond). |
| **Kiosk or shared device** (signage, library, family computer with guest mode) | Kiosk app autostarts, or several users and a guest option on the sign-in screen. | Guest-mode and sign-in restrictions matter; personal accounts left signed in are exposed to the next user. |
| **Past AUE** | About ChromeOS shows an Auto Update Expiration date in the past, or the update screen says the device no longer receives updates. | End of life: no security fixes. The usual mitigation is replacement. ChromeOS Flex is **not** a supported fix for an expired Chromebook: Flex targets certified PC and Mac models (verify on Google's certified-models list). |

## Detection

Hints for recognizing ChromeOS devices during a network inventory (used by the `full-assessment` skill).
Chromebooks expose almost no listening services by default, so network detection is weak; confirm with
the user.

- **No open ports by default.** A Chromebook in normal mode normally shows no listening TCP services to
  the LAN. An open TCP 22 suggests developer mode with SSH enabled, or a port forwarded from the Linux
  container (both are findings to confirm with the user).
- **DHCP and hostnames:** Chromebooks commonly send a DHCP hostname beginning with `chromebook` or
  similar (varies by version; not vendor-verified here). The DHCP vendor class may identify the platform.
- **Outbound traffic** to Google update and sign-in services (for example `*.google.com`,
  `*.googleapis.com`, `*.gvt1.com`), visible in router or DNS-filter logs.
- **Google Cast and mDNS:** ChromeOS browses for `_googlecast._tcp` services (it casts to TVs and
  speakers) rather than announcing its own; Nearby Share / Quick Share and Phone Hub use Bluetooth and
  local Wi-Fi.
- **MAC address vendors (OUI)** are those of the Wi-Fi module maker (for example Intel, MediaTek,
  Realtek, Qualcomm) rather than the Chromebook brand. ChromeOS can use randomized MAC addresses on
  Wi-Fi networks (verify the current setting on the device), in which case the OUI tells you nothing.
- On ChromeOS Flex, the hardware maker's NIC vendor appears, exactly as for the original operating system.

## Discover

All operations in this mode are class **R** (read-only). Confirm scope and access first (core: operating
principles). Most checks are **user-run** in Settings, in the browser, and on Google's account pages;
the agent guides and records. Mark anything you can't inspect **Not assessed**.

### Access and baseline

Ask the user for, per device:

- Make and model, whether it is a Chromebook, Chromebook Plus, Chromebox, or ChromeOS Flex install, and
  who owns it (personal, family, work, school).
- Screenshots of **Settings > About ChromeOS** (version and channel) and its **Additional details** page
  (update schedule / Auto Update Expiration date, channel, and build details). Redact serial numbers.
- Whether "This device is managed by…" appears anywhere in Settings or on the sign-in screen.
- Which Google accounts sign in to the device, which is the owner, and whether any are supervised child
  accounts.

Read-only browser pages the user can open (they show state and change nothing unless a control is
clicked). Mark each **vendor-documented** or **not yet verified** for the live version:

```text
chrome://version          # browser and OS version, channel, command-line flags (not yet verified for every build)
chrome://management       # whether the browser/device is managed, and by whom (vendor-documented)
chrome://policy           # policies in force, including force-installed extensions (vendor-documented)
chrome://extensions       # installed extensions, their source and permissions
chrome://system           # system diagnostics; contains identifiers, redact before sharing
```

- Never ask the user to open **crosh** (Ctrl+Alt+T) commands beyond read-only status, enter developer
  mode, or run `sudo` in the Linux container to "check" anything. None of the Discover checks need them.
- Network checks (port-state only, from a host the user controls, against the user's own device) are
  rarely useful but can confirm that nothing listens:

```sh
nmap -sT -Pn -p 22,5555,8000-8100 192.0.2.40   # TCP connect only; no interaction with any service
```

### Assessment domains

Every domain must end with a status in the report (Pass / Finding / Not assessed / Not applicable /
Accepted risk).

#### A. Platform, updates, and support lifetime

- ChromeOS version and channel (Stable is expected for everyday devices; Beta, Dev, and Canary trade
  stability for earlier features and are a finding on a child's or work device unless chosen
  deliberately).
- **Auto Update Expiration date** from the device's Additional details page, cross-checked against
  Google's Auto Update policy table for the model. Note whether the device is in an extended update period
  that needed an opt-in (managed devices) and whether that opt-in was made.
- Whether the device is up to date: a pending update waiting for a restart is common on devices that are
  only ever closed, not restarted. ChromeOS installs updates in the background but applies them on
  restart.
- Compare the installed version with Google's Chrome Releases blog for recent security fixes, and check
  for actively exploited Chrome or ChromeOS vulnerabilities (core triage). Don't rely on memory.
- **ChromeOS Flex:** whether the model is on Google's certified-models list, the PC's BIOS/UEFI version and
  whether the hardware maker still ships firmware updates, UEFI Secure Boot state, and whether a TPM is
  present (Flex uses it where available).
- Google has announced a move of ChromeOS onto an Android-based platform; check Google's current
  announcements for how that affects the specific device's update path before giving lifetime advice.

#### B. Verified boot, developer mode, and firmware

- Whether the device is in **developer mode** (the "OS verification is off" screen at boot, or the user
  confirms). If so: who enabled it, why, and whether it is still needed.
- In developer mode: whether a root or `chronos` password was set, whether SSH or other services were
  enabled, whether USB or legacy boot is allowed, and whether firmware write protection was removed or
  custom firmware installed. Each widens what an attacker with brief physical access can do.
- Whether the device is the user's own: a second-hand device in developer mode, or with custom firmware,
  may have been modified by a previous owner.
- **Flex:** BIOS/UEFI admin password set, boot from USB restricted, Secure Boot on (where supported).

#### C. Google account and sign-in

Assess from the user's own browser session on Google's account pages (security checkup, devices,
third-party access). Coordinate with the [mfa](../mfa/SKILL.md) skill for depth.

- 2-step verification on the owner's and every regular user's account; passkeys or security keys in
  use; recovery phone and email current; backup codes stored safely.
- **Your devices** list in the Google account: unknown or old devices still signed in (sold or lost
  Chromebooks and phones).
- **Third-party apps with account access:** OAuth grants to apps and services, especially those with
  Gmail or Drive access.
- **Device sign-in settings** (owner only): who may sign in (only listed users or anyone with a Google
  account), whether guest browsing is allowed, and whether user names and pictures show on the sign-in
  screen. On a family or child device, an unrestricted sign-in list or guest mode lets a child bypass
  supervision.
- **Screen lock:** lock when the lid closes or the device sleeps; PIN or password required to unlock;
  Smart Lock (unlock with a nearby phone) on or off and with which phone.
- Shared device: accounts left signed in that belong to people no longer using it.
- **Password manager:** whether passwords saved in Google Password Manager are protected by the account's
  2-step verification and, where offered, on-device encryption; compromised-password warnings shown in the
  Password Checkup.

#### D. Browser extensions and web content

- Every installed extension (chrome://extensions): name, publisher, source (Chrome Web Store, force-
  installed by policy, or sideloaded/"developer mode" unpacked), permissions, and whether the user knows
  why it is there.
- Flag: extensions with "read and change all your data on all websites", extensions that manage other
  extensions, proxy/VPN or "coupon" extensions the user didn't choose, unpacked extensions on a
  non-developer device, extensions removed from the Web Store or marked as malware, and extensions whose
  owner or behavior changed recently.
- **Enhanced Safe Browsing** or Standard protection on; site permissions (camera, microphone, location,
  notifications) granted to unexpected sites; notification spam from sites the user allowed by mistake.
- Isolated Web Apps and progressive web apps installed; which are expected.
- Chrome sync: what is synced, and whether a sync passphrase is used.

#### E. Android apps (Google Play)

- Whether Google Play is enabled. If so: installed apps, their permissions (camera, microphone,
  location, files, accessibility, device admin), and whether any came from outside Google Play.
- Android **developer options** and ADB debugging inside the Android environment, and whether "unknown
  sources" installs are allowed (where the platform permits it); sideloading on ChromeOS normally
  requires developer mode, so any sideloaded Android app on a non-developer device needs explaining.
- Google Play Protect on, with no warnings.
- The [phones](../phones/SKILL.md) skill's app-review checks apply.

#### F. Linux development environment (Crostini)

- Whether Linux is enabled, which user enabled it, and whether it is still used.
- The container is a full Debian system with its own packages and updates; ChromeOS updates do **not**
  update it. Check when `apt` updates were last applied (ask the user; the [linux](../linux/SKILL.md)
  skill covers the inside).
- **Port forwarding** from the container to the network (a ChromeOS Linux setting), which makes a service
  in the container reachable from the LAN. Any forwarded port is a finding to explain.
- Shared folders: which ChromeOS folders (Downloads, Google Drive) are shared into the container; a
  compromised container can read and change them.
- Microphone, camera, USB device, and GPU access granted to Linux.
- Container backups (ChromeOS offers a backup and restore for Linux); whether the container holds secrets
  such as SSH keys or cloud credentials.
- On a child-supervised or managed device: whether Linux is allowed by policy at all.

#### G. Family Link and child accounts

- The child's account is supervised (Family Link shows the Chromebook); the sign-in screen is restricted
  to listed users; guest mode is off. Otherwise the child can sign in unsupervised.
- Site filtering, app approvals for Google Play, extension installs (usually blocked or approval-only for
  supervised accounts), screen-time limits, and whether Linux and developer features are blocked.
- Parent accounts protected with 2-step verification; parents know the child's account password or can
  reset it.
- School accounts signed in on a personal device follow the school's policies, not Family Link; check
  which account the child actually uses.

#### H. Management and policy

- chrome://management and chrome://policy: managed or not, by whom, and which policies are in force.
  Unexpected management on a personal device (a browser policy installed by software, or a device the
  user believes is personal showing enterprise enrollment) is a finding and possibly an indicator.
- On a managed device the user owns personally (bought second-hand from a school or company): it may
  still be enrolled, so the previous organization can control it. Only that organization can release it;
  don't try to bypass enrollment.
- Force-installed extensions and their permissions; whether the organization's policy allows personal
  accounts or Linux on the device.
- Remote-support or remote-desktop extensions installed by policy or by the user.

#### I. Data, local storage, and network

- Local data that a powerwash would destroy: Downloads, Linux container, Android app data, offline
  files. Whether it is backed up.
- User data encryption is automatic on ChromeOS and Flex (Google documentation); the security of local
  data then rests on the account password and lock screen.
- Wi-Fi networks saved and shared between users (a network saved "shared" is available to every user of
  the device); VPNs configured; proxy settings set by an unknown party.
- Nearby Share / Quick Share visibility (everyone vs. contacts), Bluetooth pairings, and Phone Hub
  connection to the right phone.
- Physical: lost-device plan (sign out remotely via the Google account device list), privacy screen,
  camera and microphone hardware switches on models that have them.
- Disposal: devices sold or given away were removed from the Google account and powerwashed (by the
  user, at retirement).

## Recommend

No changes are made in this mode. For each finding, produce a recommendation using the core finding
template, including **Dependencies / blast radius** and the **operation class**. Describe settings by
function and give the usual menu path as a hint; tell the user to confirm the path on their version.

### Dependency and blast-radius check (required)

- **Local data:** anything in Downloads, the Linux container, or Android apps that a powerwash or
  developer-mode change would erase. Back it up first.
- **Developer workflows:** a household member may rely on developer mode or Linux for school or work;
  turning them off is a conversation, not a toggle.
- **Account changes:** adding 2-step verification or passkeys affects every device the Google account
  is signed in on, not just the Chromebook. Make sure recovery options work first.
- **Extensions:** removing a password manager, school, or accessibility extension can lock people out of
  sites or break school work.
- **Family Link changes:** restricting sign-in or guest mode affects every person who uses the device.
- **Managed devices:** changes must go through the administrator; local changes may be overwritten by
  policy.

### Recommendation guidance

| Area | Typical recommendation | Consequences to explain |
|---|---|---|
| Past AUE date | Replace the device; until then, limit it to low-risk use. | Cost; Flex is not an option for old Chromebooks. |
| Pending update / not restarted | Restart to apply updates; restart at least weekly. | A minute of downtime. |
| Non-Stable channel on a child or work device | Return to Stable. | Changing to a more stable channel may powerwash the device (verify the current behavior); back up first. |
| Developer mode not needed | Return to normal (verified) mode. | **Powerwash:** all local data lost; back up first. |
| Developer mode needed | Keep it, but set strong passwords, keep SSH off, don't remove firmware write protection, and treat the device as a developer machine. | Residual risk remains (accepted-risk candidate). |
| Owner account without 2SV | Turn on 2-step verification; prefer passkeys or a security key. | Recovery options must be set first; see the mfa skill. |
| Unknown devices in the Google account | Sign them out from the account's device list. | Signs out the listed device, including a household device chosen by mistake. |
| Unrestricted sign-in or guest mode on a child device | Restrict sign-in to listed users; disable guest browsing. | Visitors can't use the device without the owner adding them. |
| Risky or unknown extension | Remove it (or disable first, to test). | Features it provided stop. |
| Unneeded Linux or Android apps | Turn Linux off or remove unused Android apps. | Turning Linux off deletes the container; back it up. |
| Linux port forwarding on | Remove forwarded ports not actively needed. | Services in the container become unreachable from the LAN. |
| Container not updated | Update packages inside the container regularly. | Normal Linux update risks. |
| Second-hand managed device | Ask the seller or previous organization to release it, or return it. | The organization can otherwise keep controlling the device. |
| Flex without firmware support | Update firmware from the maker, enable Secure Boot and a firmware password, or plan replacement. | Firmware updates carry their own risk; follow the maker's procedure. |

Group the plan: immediate containment (if any) → urgent fixes (past-AUE devices, unexplained developer
mode or management, account takeover risk) → high-priority hardening (2SV, extensions, sign-in
restrictions) → routine maintenance (restarts, Linux updates) → optional defense in depth. Then ask for
approval (core: modes and authorization).

---

## Remediate

Apply only approved changes, one at a time, following the core rules. The user makes the changes while
the agent guides and verifies from screenshots. ChromeOS specifics:

- **Back up before any powerwash or developer-mode change.** Confirm Downloads, Linux, and Android data
  are copied off the device or synced. Leaving developer mode and powerwash are **C3** for local data.
- **Settings toggles** (guest mode, sign-in restriction, Safe Browsing, Nearby Share visibility, Linux
  port forwarding) are usually **C1**: screenshot the old value first.
- **Removing extensions or Android apps is C2** (C3 if app data matters); disable an extension first to
  test the effect, then remove.
- **Google account changes** (2SV, passkeys, signing out devices, removing third-party access) are
  **C2**: they affect every device on the account. Do them from a trusted device, and confirm recovery
  options work before tightening sign-in.
- **Turning Linux off is C3** for the container; use the built-in Linux backup first if the data
  matters.
- **Channel changes** may powerwash the device; treat them as C3 for local data unless the live
  documentation says otherwise.
- **Managed devices:** don't make or suggest changes that policy forbids; route them to the
  administrator.

After each change, follow the core "after a change" steps: re-screenshot the setting, confirm the user can
still sign in and work, and record before and after.

### Hard stops (refer to a specialist or the owner; never automate)

- Bypassing, removing, or "unenrolling" enterprise or school management without the organization.
- Removing firmware write protection, flashing custom or third-party firmware, or installing another
  operating system as a security fix.
- Entering developer mode to "investigate" a suspected compromise.
- Running recovery-media creation or a recovery that wipes the device while an incident is open and
  evidence is still needed (see Respond).
- Signing in to the user's Google account or handling their passwords, recovery codes, or passkeys.

## Respond

On any P0 indicator (developer mode or "OS verification is off" that nobody enabled, unexpected
management or policies on a personal device, extensions nobody installed, Google account security alerts
or sign-ins nobody recognizes, a changed account password or recovery option, or a device behaving as if
someone else is controlling it), switch to Respond immediately. Follow the core playbook plus the
ChromeOS-specific steps in [incident-response.md](incident-response.md).

## Worked example (invented)

### CROS-001: Family Chromebook in developer mode with guest browsing allowed

**Confidence:** Confirmed
**Priority:** P2. Verified boot is off, so a modified operating system would still boot, and anyone
with a few minutes of physical access can get a root shell; guest mode lets the child bypass Family Link
supervision. Not internet-exposed, so not P1.
**State:** Open
**Component:** Chromebook used by the household's children; ChromeOS Stable channel, version as shown on
the user's screenshot; Auto Update Expiration date several years in the future.
**Evidence:** User-provided photo, 2026-04-02: "OS verification is off" screen at boot. Screenshot of
Settings > Security and privacy > Manage other people: guest browsing on, sign-in not restricted. The
user says an older child enabled developer mode last year to try a game launcher and no longer uses it.
A TCP connect port-state check from `192.0.2.50` showed no listening ports on `192.0.2.41` (observed).
**Expected secure state:** normal (verified) mode; sign-in restricted to listed users; guest browsing
off on a supervised child's device (Google Chromebook and Family Link help).
**Exposure and prerequisites:** physical access to the device; or the child choosing guest mode.
**Dependencies / blast radius:** leaving developer mode powerwashes the device; the child has drawings
in Downloads that aren't backed up. No Linux or developer workflow in use.
**Recommended remediation:** copy Downloads to Google Drive; restrict sign-in and turn off guest
browsing; then return to verified mode (powerwash) and sign the child back in under supervision.
**Operation class:** C1 for the sign-in settings; C3 for the developer-mode exit (local data erased).
**Approval required:** Yes, separately for each.
**Verification:** no "OS verification is off" screen on the next boot; sign-in screen shows only listed
users and no guest option; Family Link shows the device as supervised.
**Rollback:** sign-in settings can be restored from the screenshot. Developer mode can be re-enabled
(not recommended); the powerwash itself can't be undone, which is why the backup comes first.
